chunks.text: Caryota urens — the solitary fishtail palm, toddy palm or jaggery palm — is native to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Malaysia and India, growing as a single unbranched trunk up to about 18 m with a strikingly jagged-edged, bipinnate crown roughly 6 m across; its Sanskrit name moha-karin, 'delusion maker', and Latin epithet urens, 'stinging', both reference the oxalic acid in its fruit, which irritates skin and mucous membranes if handled raw. Unusually among palms, it is hapaxanthic (monocarpic): it flowers and fruits progressively along its trunk over several years and then dies once that cycle completes. Its sap is the source of Sri Lanka's prized kithul treacle, a thick dark syrup made by boiling the sap for many hours, as well as toddy, a fermented palm wine tapped from the flower stalk that in parts of western India is further distilled into a traditional liquor called maadi. The pulp of the mature trunk is sun-dried and powdered into a sweet, nutritious food in coastal Karnataka, the trunk's starchy heart resembles sago, the young growing shoot ('cabbage') is eaten as a vegetable, and its strong leaf fibre is used for basketry in Cambodia. In a sign of its continuing cultural weight, Sri Lanka's traditional kithul-tapping industry was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 11 December 2025.

This Sri Lankan tourism-industry source adds texture to the human side of the kithul economy: it describes the industry as a genuine 'money-spinner for the rural masses', with tapping skills passed down within families as closely guarded trade secrets, and a single successfully tapped inflorescence yielding sap continuously for eight to ten months at a rate of roughly 20-30 bottles of sap per day. A tapped tree, the source claims, can earn a household around Rs. 10,000 (about US$34) a month — a meaningful cottage-industry income for families with few other options — and skilled tappers are described as held in high regard within their communities as masters of an inherited craft. The source dates the tradition back some 2,000 years, describing kithul treacle and jaggery as sweeteners central enough to ancient Ceylon's economy that they were historically bartered directly for staples such as paddy rice, pulses, vegetables and meat. As with most tourism-oriented sources, its economic figures and health claims should be treated as self-reported rather than independently verified, but the broad picture — of a long-standing, still-active rural livelihood built entirely around this single palm species — lines up with the more cautious academic and encyclopedic accounts.
